> 「云何为人演说？不取于相，如如不动。」「一切有为法，如梦幻泡影，如露亦如电，应作如是观。」佛说是经已……皆大欢喜，信受奉行。

The last section asks how to hand this on, answers in seven characters, and closes with six metaphors.

云何为人演说 — how should one explain it to others?
不取于相，如如不动 — not grasping at marks; unmoved, in suchness.

Then the verse that ends the sutra, and is probably its most quoted passage:

一切有为法，如梦幻泡影，如露亦如电，应作如是观.

All conditioned things are like a dream, an illusion, a bubble, a shadow; like dew, and like lightning. Thus should they be seen.

## 不取于相 is the method of transmission

The question is not "what should I say". It is how to speak — and the answer is a posture, not a content.

Whoever explains this while grasping at marks will transmit the grasping. The listener learns the shape of the speaker's attachment more reliably than the speaker's words. Which is why the sutra's instruction for teaching is indistinguishable from its instruction for living.

## 如如不动 is not immobility

如如 — suchness doubled: thus, thus. 不动 — unmoved.

The book is explicit: this is not rigidity or numbness. It is the nature not being dragged by the arising and passing of appearances. The body moves, the voice changes, the situation is met; the ground does not shift because there was no ground to shift.

Anyone who has tried to be unmoved by suppressing reaction knows the cost: the reaction continues underneath, and the effort of hiding it becomes the main activity. 如如不动 has no hidden layer to manage.

## The six metaphors are not one metaphor

Dream, illusion, bubble, shadow, dew, lightning.

They are often run together as a single sentiment — "things are unreal" — but each has a different edge:

- Dream: vivid while occurring, and made of the mind that dreams it.
- Illusion: an appearance produced by a trick, functioning perfectly until the trick is seen.
- Bubble: formed from something insubstantial, brief, and easily burst.
- Shadow: dependent entirely on something else to cast it.
- Dew: present at dawn, gone by mid-morning.
- Lightning: brilliant, instantaneous, and gone before it is located.

Six angles on one fact: appearing, and not able to be held.

## 应作如是观

Not "believe this". 观 — contemplate, view, look at it this way.

An instruction about seeing, offered at the end, after thirty-one sections of dismantling. Which is the sutra's shape: it never asks for assent. It asks you to look, and keeps removing what you were looking from.

## 皆大欢喜，信受奉行

The sutra ends with the assembly rejoicing and putting it into practice.

信受奉行: believe, receive, and carry out. The three verbs in order, and the third is the one that decides whether the other two happened.

## Closing this series

Thirty-two sections, one post each, each canonical to its own page. The book behind them is 润泽说 道可道之金刚经, with a section-by-section commentary, a glossary of the terms that resist translation, and five appendices.

If you have read all thirty-two, you have read the sutra once through — and noticed that the instruction never changed. It arrived in section one as a man washing his feet, and it leaves in section thirty-two as six metaphors for lightning.

The instruction is the same in both: do not stand on it.

## The test

Take one thing you are certain is real, and hold it against the six metaphors. Not to conclude that it is nothing — the sutra has spent thirty-one sections refusing that conclusion.

Just to notice which one fits. Dream, illusion, bubble, shadow, dew, lightning.

One of them will fit better than you expect, and the fitting is the whole of 如是观.
